stories.title: Healey to ask EU finance ministers to let UK into Made in Europe scheme
stories.summary: The chancellor wants the Made in Europe programme to deepen ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
John Healey is meeting EU finance ministers on Friday

Published 17 September 2026

The chancellor is to warn the European Union (EU) not to lock the UK out of its scheme to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

John Healey will push for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday.

But he will call on the EU to design its "Made in Europe" programme in a way that deepens ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers", Treasury sources told the BBC.

Officials said Healey will tell European finance ministers it is important to "learn lessons" after talks collapsed last year for Britain to join an EU defence loans scheme.

That dispute centred on how much money the UK would pay to join.

The "Made in Europe" policy, officially called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), is currently being considered by the bloc and aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries.

There is concern in government the scheme could lock British firms out of European supply chains.

Treasury officials said Healey wanted to reduce the economic impact of Brexit and build closer ties with the EU, but not at any cost to the UK.

Former UK trade negotiator Sir Crawford Falconer said the EU's original plan would have allowed free trade partners - such as the UK - to be included in the scheme but a subsequent proposal recommended limiting membership to EU nations.

Sir Crawford said that caused "everyone to hit the panic button," adding: "If we weren't able to complete on equal terms, it would put the viability of some of our production facilities at risk."

Earlier this year, the Nissan car company said: "EU and UK manufacturing are deeply intertwined, and restricting eligibility for public support to EU only assembly would damage competitiveness, disrupt integrated supply chains, and undermine Europe's EV transition."

Healey said: "The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places.

"To me, closer ties with the EU means British businesses – wherever they are based across the UK – get better access to both the supply chains and the customers they need to grow."

Healey will use the meeting in Dublin to focus on tech firms, defence companies, and manufacturing.

"The chancellor wants to make sure nothing holds them back," a Treasury source said.

It comes after a reset summit with the EU was delayed after Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister.

Treasury sources now expect that to take place in November.

Healey's meeting in Dublin comes after it emerged earlier this week that he is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending.

He is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.

Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.

Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review.

stories.summary: What the plan to sell £146bn in gilts back to the Treasury means for the public finances Bank of England holds interest rates Burnham’s talk of ‘breathing space’ at odds with reality of future rate rises Mixed in with the Bank of England’s decision on Thursday to hold interest rates at 3.75% was a surprise announcement that it was shaking up its programme of quantitative tightening. So why is this apparently arcane change to QT important, and what does it mean for the public finances? Continue reading...
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
What the plan to sell £146bn in gilts back to the Treasury means for the public finances

Bank of England holds interest rates

Burnham’s talk of ‘breathing space’ at odds with reality of future rate rises

Mixed in with the Bank of England’s decision on Thursday to hold interest rates at 3.75% was a surprise announcement that it was shaking up its programme of quantitative tightening.

So why is this apparently arcane change to QT important, and what does it mean for the public finances?

What is QT?

It is the Bank of England’s controversial process of selling off hundreds of billions of pounds worth of government bonds that it bought via the emergency policy of quantitative easing (QE) during the financial crises of 2008 and Covid.

The Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) sees QT as the necessary unwinding of the massive balance sheet it built up. Its stockpile of bonds, known as gilts, has already been reduced from a peak of £895bn in February 2022, to £488bn.

But critics on the right and left have complained that selling off significant quantities of government bonds costs the Treasury, as they are being sold at a loss.

There have also been concerns that in a febrile bond market , large-scale sell-offs risk depressing prices – and thus driving up the yield, or interest rate, the government has to pay to borrow.

What is the Bank looking to change?

Instead of looking for private-sector buyers for its stock of gilts, the Bank plans to sell them directly to the Treasury instead.

The Treasury’s debt management office (DMO), which has the job of doing the government’s borrowing for it, will then issue new bonds to cover the costs of those it has bought from the Bank.

The Treasury sees this as simplifying what can be a messy process. As the chancellor, John Healey, put it in a letter to the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, on Thursday: “This sales model … would see a return to a single public-sector supplier of gilts to the market.”

It also has the advantage of allowing the DMO to tailor gilt sales to market demand, which currently favour gilts that mature over a shorter period, rather than the Bank having to sell off the 20- and 30-year dated gilts it still has on its books, for which there is less investor appetite.

The yield, effectively the interest rate, on 30-year gilts dropped sharply on Thursday after the decision was announced, to 5.745% – and was on course for its biggest drop since 2020.

No final decision has been made, however, despite the fact the Treasury, Bank and DMO have apparently been discussing the idea for a year. Healey has promised to make a final ruling in April – and until then, QT will be paused.

Wasn’t QT already being slowed down?

Yes. The Bank has run down its stock of gilts by £70bn this year . That included £20bn of actual sales; and another £50bn worth that reached their maturity date.

Over the coming years, it plans to sell off £20bn of government bonds annually, alongside retiring gilts that reach maturity.

That’s because the Bank is keen to avoid the risks of exacerbating already-fragile bond markets . The minutes of the MPC meeting revealed that members discussed offloading bonds at a faster rate; but “at a time when bond markets globally had been volatile, this risked destabilising markets”.

The Bank also announced it would set aside about £120bn of the longest-dated government bonds it holds, as these are used to back the issuance of the UK’s bank notes.

In total, the Bank expects to sell a total of £146bn of gilts between now and 2034 – at a steady pace of £20bn a year – back to the government, if Healey gives the plan the thumbs up.

What’s the impact for the public finances?

Analysts expect it to be modest. The Treasury may be able to finance its borrowing a bit more cheaply when the Bank is not selling a slew of long-dated bonds into the market. As analysts at the investment bank Jefferies put it: “Taken together, the changes imply a materially lower future supply burden, particularly for [long-dated gilts].”

And to the extent that the pace of sales is slowing, the losses on those bonds, which is borne by the Treasury, will crystallise more slowly – another marginal upside.

Jefferies also suggested that, by making its future plans clear, the MPC’s decision could “ease some of the pressure that had been building for changes to the Bank’s QT approach”.

stories.title: 'Don't be silly' over Falklands and Irish unity, top Tory tells Trump
stories.summary: Shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat says the US president's recent comments were aimed at US voters, in a BBC interview.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Tom Tugendhat was appointed Tory shadow foreign secretary earlier this month

Published 8 hours ago

The shadow foreign secretary has told Donald Trump "don't be silly" over his comments on the UK's sovereignty of the Falkland Islands and Irish reunification.

Conservative MP Tom Tugendhat said the US president was trying to appeal to voters at home by making comments about the British overseas territory in the Atlantic Ocean and saying he would "love" to see a united Ireland.

Trump has said America's position on the Falklands is "one of many" under review, and hinted he would not help the UK in any potential future conflict with Argentina.

And the US president said on a visit to Ireland last week that Irish reunification was "going to happen eventually" and it would be a "great thing".

Britain and Argentina still dispute the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, four decades on from an armed conflict there which the UK won.

Argentina's president heightened tensions with the UK over the Falkland Islands earlier this month, saying in a presidential address that "winds of change" favoured his country's claim to the islands.

He warned he will impose economic sanctions on firms which exploit oil nearby.

In response, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK's position on the islands was "unwavering", and they would remain British as "that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders."

And Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has hit back strongly over the issue, insisting "the Falkland Islands are British" and that Britain's continued connection with them "is of vital importance".

But Tugendhat, the Tory MP for Tonbridge in Kent who Badenoch appointed her shadow foreign secretary in a reshuffle earlier this month, has suggested Trump does not mean it.

"What he's doing is he's bumping his gums on some issues that he thinks are supportive to various electoral issues for himself at home," he told Nick Robinson on Political Thinking.

"He's got elections coming up in November, he knows he's got votes to win.

"Is it helpful to us? No. But this is his politics, not ours. So sometimes we have to say something and sometimes we have to go, 'come on mate, don't be silly'."

Political Thinking with Nick Robinson

Nick Robinson has a conversation with, not an interrogation of, the people who shape our political thinking about what shaped theirs.

Tugendhat explained that Britain's military capability in the Falklands is radically different from in 1982, when the UK and Argentina fought for 74 days over the territory, with the UK Foreign Office not negotiating to give the islands up in recent years.

And asked about Trump saying he would "love to see" Irish reunification on a recent trip there, Tugendhat branded this "plain old electioneering," ahead of US mid-term elections in November.

"Is he going to do anything about it? No," he added.

Chinese sanctions

Elsewhere in his interview, Tugendhat revealed he had received no confirmation from China that the country's sanctions against him had been dropped.

This is despite then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer announcing they had been in January.

He said he would only visit China, whose communist regime he has long criticised, if there was something relevant and worth discussing - but he feels talks can be held elsewhere at the moment.

He also said Miliband should have waited rather than showing "weakness" after the UK sanctioned illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

And he ruled out bringing Britain back into the European Union if in government, despite his close personal ties to the continent including his French wife who was influential in the recent Bayeux Tapestry exchange.

Having run against Badenoch for Tory leader in 2022, he praised her performance as leader so far - saying her hoping to be Britain's next prime minister was a weight off his own shoulders.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sam Battle, performing as Look Mum No Computer, finished in last place at the 2026 Eurovision Song Contest with one point for his song "Eins, Zwei, Drei"

Published 8 hours ago

The UK's "dismal" record in selecting songs and acts for Eurovision is to be scrutinised by MPs.

In May, Look Mum No Computer came last with one point. In 2023 Mae Muller finished second from bottom and in 2021 James Newman came last - this time with "nul points".

The act that represents the UK is selected by the BBC, sometimes with a record label or music management company.

The chair of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee, Dame Caroline Dinenage, said: "We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant, on what basis and whether our dismal record of achievement in recent years [Sam Ryder to one side] is the result of bad song choice, weak performance... or something else".

James Newman came last with song Embers, scoring "nul points" in 2021

It's expected that figures from the BBC, as well as music industry experts, will be called to give evidence to the committee of cross-party MPs at a hearing that will be held "over the coming months". The committee is also likely to receive relevant written submissions.

UK music success rarely repeated at Eurovision

Although the UK has, over the years, produced some of the world's most successful artists, that kind of success has rarely been repeated at Eurovision .

Over the past 15 years, the UK has only come higher than 15th place on one occasion - when Sam Ryder came second with his song Space Man in 2022. He was beaten by Ukraine's Kalush Orchestra.

And next year's event, being held in Burgas in Bulgaria, will mark 30 years since the UK last won the contest, when Katrina and the Waves scored 227 points with their song Love Shine A Light.

Many countries choose their entry through a publicly televised selection process.

The last time this was done in the UK was with the show Eurovision: You Decide in 2019. Michael Rice was selected, but went on to come last at the contest in Tel Aviv, Israel.

Success story Sam Ryder finished second at Eurovision 2022...

... while Katrina and the Waves were the last UK act to win Eurovision, in 1997

The MPs' hearing will be part of the committee's State of Play inquiry, where members of the public or others can request an evidence session to be held into a particular subject that interests or concerns them.

Dame Caroline told BBC News: "This application interested us because of the UK's reputation for scoring 'nul points', coming bottom, or close to bottom in recent years at Eurovision, despite having world-class song writers and musicians."

The Eurovision final has consistently been one of the UK's most popular music events, with millions staying up late to watch the final result.

No time frame for the select committee hearing has been set yet, but once all the evidence has been examined, it's expected that the committee may produce a short report containing recommendations to the BBC.

stories.title: Not just 'Nice Guy Eddie': Lib Dems eager for leader to show radical side at party conference
stories.summary: There is a sizeable group of Lib Dem MPs who openly question whether the party's problem is with its leader, while others support his stance.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 18 September 2026, 01:18 BST

Discontent bubbles not far from the surface as the Liberal Democrats gather for their conference this weekend.

Two years on from their best ever general election result, conversations with those on the party's frontbench, its MPs, and backroom staff reveal a frustration at what many see as a failure to capitalise on that success.

Polling by YouGov in the build up to the conference highlighted the Lib Dems "have seen no real growth in support since the last general election" and if anything have slipped back.

"We lack the ability to say something new or interesting," said one senior Lib Dem MP.

"There is no energy, no excitement."

A frontbencher said: "With the possible exception of our position on Trump, you could characterise most of our press lines as 'a Lib Dem spokesperson said, steady on now, gently does it'."

Others describe the party's approach as "boring" and are spooked by the rise of the Green Party under Zack Polanski.

The party's leadership are aware of the anger. They insist this conference will be a "gear shift".

Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader, told me it would be "a gloves-off kind of conference".

"You'll see a bit of fighting talk," she said.

Some of the caution until now has been deliberate. The party's leadership met over the last few months and discussed whether to copy Polanski's punchy, social media-focused style but decided it wouldn't appeal to the well-heeled areas of southern England that form the Lib Dem heartlands.

Those involved in that decision point to Polanski's recent struggles and feel vindicated.

But at all levels of the party there is an acknowledgement they lag behind other parties on grabbing attention on social media, highlighted by Andy Burnham's "social first" approach.

The party has only recently rolled out training for its MPs on making social videos, something senior figures despair at.

"When we have a success we're very good at getting a leaflet sent out to supporters straight away," one senior MP said. "But we don't do that for socials."

Digital and social media will be a focus of at least 17 fringe events at conference, as the party tries to improve its online communications.

But others worry that social media is just the medium and the problem is with the message.

'We need to be angry'

One MP raised the majority of voters (52% according to YouGov,) who view the party as "weak" in recent polling; and the tendency to say it's unclear what the party stands for (43% believing the party was weak, to 18% thinking it was strong).

"We need to become bolder and more radical," a senior MP added. "We need to be angry on behalf of our constituents."

Another Lib Dem MP said: "We are stuck fighting the guerilla politics of local campaigning. There is no broader articulation of what a vision for Liberal Britain is."

Even those most loyal to Davey admit the party was struggling to offer a clear and coherent message. The Lib Dems' success at the last general election was, the party's own strategists believe, because voters wanted to remove the Conservatives and the Lib Dems benefitted from that anti-Tory sentiment.

"We haven't yet answered why people should vote for us rather than against the Tories," admitted one senior advisor.

In public, Lib Dem MPs are often coy about the possibility of a coalition government with Labour after the election. In private, there are no such reservations.

In an election many think could produce a hung parliament with no party in overall majority, the Lib Dem ambition is to be kingmakers to block a Reform government.

"If you're a serious political party you exist to be in government," the same senior adviser said.

Lib Dem strategists are confident they can retain most of the 72 seats they won in 2024. Their sights now are on the 27 others where they came second, most of which were won by the Conservatives.

The party made gains in the May local elections in England

The party's leadership characterise the last two years since the general election as "stage one" when a largely new intake of MPs bedded into their constituencies.

"Stage two is winning the air war and describing exactly what Liberal Britain looks like. You'll see a lot of that at conference," said Cooper.

Of her boss, party leader Sir Ed, she said: "He's not just nice guy Eddie. I think you're going to see him being a bit more gritty because he's a real fighter."

She added Davey saw the battle with Reform UK as the "fight of our lives".

Critics within the party point out that promise of fighting talk to take on Reform UK accompanied the last Lib Dem conference . Yet little has changed in the party's national standings.

Join EU migration pact to tackle small boats, says Ed Davey Published 18 August

Change voting system before next election, Davey urges Burnham Published 14 July

Lib Dems offer alternative to extremes of Reform and Greens, Davey says Published 9 May

There is a sizeable group of Lib Dem MPs, and members of its frontbench, who openly question whether their problem is not with the message, nor the strategy, but with Davey, the leader.

"I think he's holding us back," said one of the party's spokespeople who is planning a tilt at the leadership if a race is triggered.

"The atmosphere is ripe for a leadership challenge," another MP, talking of the frustrations in the party, said.

"But we don't have a Wes Streeting," they added, referring to Labour's defence secretary whose challenge to Sir Keir Starmer undermined his leadership.

"There is a lack of an ambitious, young alternative putting themselves out there to show a different way."

Davey's supporters in the party point to his experience of government and insist there is no one better to replace him. They also dismiss national polling as the way to measure the Lib Dem's standing.

"I'd like to be on more than 10% [in national opinion polls]," one frontbencher loyal to Davey said. "But I'd prefer to be on 10% and looking at winning 80 seats than on 15% and winning four."

"You look at our ground game and you look at our local election results," another said, pointing to gains the party made at this year's May elections. "That shows you that our strategy is definitely working."

But frustration bubbles away. And plenty in the party are looking at alternatives to Davey, like the party's President Josh Babarinde or Cooper, and question why they aren't setting out alternative visions.

Both will give speeches at the conference, as will the home affairs spokesperson Max Wilkinson.

So what of Cooper, who many consider the frontrunner to succeed Davey?

"Ed is absolutely the right leader," she tells me. "I really like being deputy leader to Ed. We work together as a team. I think we complement each other."

Would she want to be leader? "There is no vacancy," she says.

Ever? "There is no vacancy at the moment," she replies.

stories.title: War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?
stories.summary: The military and government say the risk of conflict is growing, but we may not be mentally ready for it

stories.body:
War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?

Published 18 September 2026, 00:22 BST

If the UK suddenly found itself at war, would you know what to do? Do you know what would be expected of you?

The government wants us all to start preparing for severe disruption to our lives. It wants us to stockpile canned food and drinking water, strengthen our civic resilience, and plan for the possibility of war.

Work has begun on the government's so-called "war book", which hasn't been updated in decades.

The UK's most senior soldier has sounded the alarm. The Chief of the Defence Staff Sir Richard Knighton this week said the threat from Russia meant Britain was living through the "most dangerous" period of his 35-year career in the armed forces.

But what is the threat? In 1940 the danger of a German invasion of the UK was very real. But the chances of Russian tanks rolling up Whitehall are surely negligible.

"It's not the tanks you need to worry about," says historian Margaret MacMillan, author of War: How Conflict Shaped Us.

"It's the cutting of cables on the ocean floor. It's the hacking into systems on which so many things depend. The possibility for asymmetric war, for cyber war, is growing by leaps and bounds."

But are we ready? After 80 years without war on our own soil, are we, as a society, psychologically prepared for it? Are we ready to approve large increases in defence spending, and for the sacrifices that that might entail in other areas of our national life? Or does the threat seem too far-fetched to be real?

The Great War legacy

"I think we have become used to the idea that peace is the normal state of affairs, that it's going to last," says McMillan.

"So no, I don't think we are psychologically prepared… but I do think that we are beginning to recognise that war is something that is closer to us than we'd like to think".

Archive film footage showing Britons in 1913 enjoying days at the races or watching the cricket contrasts sharply with what followed during the horrors of World War One.

The summer before World War One has come to symbolise a lack of readiness for war

"In a sense it's now a bit like those Edwardian summers before 1914, when there was a lot of talk of war but the notion of actually going to war seemed so far-fetched as to be beyond belief and I think that's where we are at the moment," says retired British General Sir Richard Shirreff, a former Deputy Supreme Allied Commander Europe.

Europe has not always been so war-averse. In 1914, recruitment stations were flooded with volunteers eager to serve their country. In Britain, that generation was raised on heroic tales of empire-building, in which war was one glorious cavalry charge, leading to swift victory and everyone home by Christmas.

But the experience of what came to be known as the Great War seared itself into the popular consciousness and survives in our collective imagination.

One in eight of the men who enlisted in the UK left their bones in the fields of Flanders and France, Mesopotamia and Gallipoli. The survivors carved their unspeakable grief into the landscape with the erection of thousands of war memorials. The pain of it touched every community in the land.

The horrors of the war touched every part of society

That conflict, says Margaret MacMillan, changed fundamentally the way Europe thought about war.

"The experience of the First World War showed just how dreadful modern war is… And the idea that war could be glamorous never really came back after that."

A crisis of disbelief

Europeans, and especially Western Europe's leadership elites, have succumbed to a decades-long "crisis of disbelief", argues Andrew Michta, a Polish-born American academic who is professor of strategic studies at the Hamilton School, University of Florida.

He argues that the UK, in common with many European nations, has very low levels of psychological preparedness, and that authorities are not being candid about the looming threats.

"The Germans have totally disarmed during the last 30 years. The UK is also largely disarmed and, most importantly, mentally. There is no readiness for what's happening because the policy elites are not addressing their publics in a way that would honestly state the gravity of the situation," Michta says.

When the Soviet Union collapsed in the early 1990s, many European countries began a decades-long winding down of military preparedness, dramatically cutting defence spending, in the belief that the threat from Russia had disappeared.

Michta singles out Germany's heavy reliance on Russian energy via the Nord Stream gas pipelines - which transported huge quantities of gas from Russia to Germany under the Baltic Sea - in what he sees as the mistaken belief that Berlin could manage its relationship with Moscow via political and economic means.

"So you've lived through 20 years of appeasement in Europe driven by the elites' lack of willingness or courage… to articulate how the situation was changing and how rapidly."

General Sir Richard Shirreff argues that Russia's initial invasion of Ukraine in 2014 was the real turning point, the moment Russia revealed itself as a tenacious threat to western security.

"The reality is that Russia believes it's been at war with Nato since 2014. Not a conventional war, but a war designed to undermine the integrity of target states or alliances.

"I would never take the Russians for granted. It would not be beyond the realms of possibility for them to try to unhinge Nato by, for example, attempting to take over Spitsbergen [in the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard] or something else indirect.

"So that's what we need to be prepared for".

Richard Knighton says this moment is freighted with danger

Mounting calls for increases in defence spending are rooted in a belief that the best way to prevent a war is to be ready - psychologically and militarily - to fight one. Not everyone agrees.

The belief that we are under threat is key, says psychologist Jim Orford, professor emeritus of clinical and community psychology at the University of Birmingham. "It is what I call simplistic thinking. In order to contemplate the possibility of going to war we've got to think in simplistic terms. In terms of enemies and heroes. We've got to think of Russia as an enemy. The narratives are all simplified.

"Being [psychologically] prepared for war is the first stage. Contemplating war is the second phase and then actually engaging in war is the third. I think we're well into the 'contemplating war' phase."

Citizen engagement

This "crisis of disbelief", as Michta put it, is not evenly spread. The further east you go, the closer you get to the Russian border, the more alert a nation's people are to the threat, and the more psychologically prepared.

Sweden hasn't had a war in 200 years. It has pursued a policy of neutrality for centuries. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it abandoned that and has made itself, in a very short space of time, one of the most psychologically prepared countries in Europe.

"Russia is self-evidently dangerous", Sweden's outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Christersson told The Economist magazine last month.

"We don't know when it [the war in Ukraine] ends, but how it ends will define the security situation in our part of the world for at least a generation"

Sweden has a system of partial conscription, in which all school leavers must register for military service. The armed forces pick - and conscript - the best candidates. The conscripts then do up to 15 months compulsory training before going back into civilian life, in employment or higher education. At the same time, they become part of their country's large reserve force.

"There's a lot of citizen engagement," says Minna Alander, an analyst at the Stockholm Centre for Eastern European Studies think tank. "It was almost an internet joke in 2022 and 2023 that everybody wished for a call up. Sometimes people get frustrated if they haven't been called up for a long time. It's an expectation for sure.

"Sweden has, for example, been identifying civil engineers with some relevant skills in, say, electricity supply who could be exercised in case of disruption. So Sweden can access this pool of civil engineers [who know] what they could do and how they could be activated."

When Christersson was asked whether Russia should be seen as a potential aggressor even after the war in Ukraine is over he said, "Yes. We have a few hundred years experience of this… We know Russia pretty well."

The three Baltic Republics - Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia - also know Russia pretty well. They only regained their independence from Moscow in the 1990s. German troops invaded Lithuania in the 1940s and are now back on Lithuanian soil, this time by invitation, to bolster that country's defences against the threat from the east. A thousand British troops lead a multi-national force in Estonia for the same reason.

Finnish troops fought hard against Russia during World War Two

But it is to the Finns that much of Europe now looks for lessons in mass psychological preparedness and civic resilience.

Finland's approach to defence and security is also rooted in historical experience. Of the 100,000 Nordic citizens who died in the World War Two, 90% were from Finland. They died in the so-called Winter War of 1939-40 against the Soviet Union. This tiny country repelled an attack by its giant neighbour and retained its independence.

Finland today shares an 800-mile (1,287km) border with Russia. After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Finland also quickly abandoned its historic neutrality and joined Nato along with its neighbour Sweden.

Finland has universal male conscription, and some women also volunteer to serve. When their service is complete they then become part of Finland's reserve force. This has the effect of closing the gap between the professional military and the civilian population.

"If conscription is done well, it ties every single family into national security thinking. Your grandfather, your great-grandfather and your sons, they all go to the same military service," says the retired three-star General Arto Raty, a former permanent secretary of Finland's Ministry of Defence.

"We bind the whole of society into supporting the military. Every single hospital has its crisis tasking. Every water supply agency. And interestingly, the most publicly trusted organisations in Finland today are the military, the defence forces and the police. That is not the case in most countries."

The Finnish military also runs a series of courses annually for leaders of society - MPs, government ministers, the CEOs of private enterprises and public utilities, the health service, even NGOs and the churches.

"We train them in crisis management, so that they understand how society will work in a crisis. We've been doing it every year since 1960."

Finland, with a population of 5.5 million, has a professional defence force of 23,000. That compares to Britain's 70,000 from a population of 66 million. But it also has a trained reserve force of close to 1 million and can mobilise a reserve army of 280,000 at short notice.

Finland has a large trained reserve force

In 2025, Finland spent 2.5% of its GDP on defence, comparable to the 2.3% spent by the UK the same year.

Should the rest of Europe go to the expense of following Finland's lead when the prospects of a conventional war with Russia seem vanishingly remote?

"An army of 70,000 is simply not going to cut the mustard in the sort of war we are going to have to face," says Gen Sir Richard Shirreff. "So I don't see how we could generate the military capability needed without some form of call-up."

He says the Norwegian model might be one that helps change the British mindset around war.

"There, every school leaver is registered for conscription… and they go and do a year's training after which they go on to university and when, later, they are competing for jobs, if they've got national service on their CV, they're seen as the best candidates… That's the sort of thing we should look at."

He adds: "The case has to be made honestly by political leaders who must really look the population in the eye and say 'this has got to be done for us to be secure'."

'Software issue to blame' for UK flight disruption

Newsflash: British air traffic control operator Nats has reveale that the outage which affected hundreds of thousands of passengers last week was due to a software defect.

In a report into the disruption, Nats also dismisses claims that the disruption was caused by “military intervention.”

Martin Rolfe, Nats chief executive officer, says:

double quotation mark “This was a software issue in a specific part of our flight data system, that we have traced to a small subsection of coding. The issue has been identified and mitigation is in place while a permanent fix is safety tested and deployed.”

The Financial Times reported last week that four people briefed on the incident claimed that the shutdown was caused by a flight plan submitted by a UK military aircraft.

NATS, though, is blaming “a software defect” in a small part of the National Airspace System (NAS), which is used to manage of UK airspace.

Hundreds of thousands of passengers were caught up in the disruption which began on Tuesday 8 September.

The software in question allocates codes to individual aircraft when manual requests are made; these are usually allocated automatically. These codes are used to identify flights on radar when they are airborne.

This glitch led to restrictions being put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety. Although the software issue only affected flights in the London Area Control centre – higher level flights operating mainly above 24,500ft – the restrictions had to be placed across the UK so that the NAS could be restarted and flight data reloaded, it says.

Heidi Alexander: air traffic disruption completely unacceptable

The government asked the UK’s civil aviation authority to check Nats’s report into its systems outage.

Heidi Alexander, the UK’s transport secretary, says:

double quotation mark “The disruption we saw last week was completely unacceptable and I know how frustrating it was for passengers, airlines and airports. “I have now received NATS’ report and, while I am pleased to see that the safety of passengers was protected, it’s clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos. I have therefore tasked the CAA with conducting an independent review to check NATS’ findings and investigate their investment plans to enhance resilience in the future, along with regulatory accountability. “It is crucial that our national infrastructure is fit for the future, and this government will make sure the aviation sector is as resilient as possible, so passengers can get to where they need to be.”

Martin Rolfe has also apologised for the disruption caused after Nats’s system outage, saying:

double quotation mark "I would like to apologise again, very sincerely, to everyone who was affected last week. It’s our job to get people where they want to go, quickly and without delay and we are devastated when that goes wrong. However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question.”

European stock markets are on the back foot today too, as investors ponder a world of rising interest rates.

In London, the FTSE 100 share index is down 1.2% or 129 points at 10,685 points, with retailers among the fallers despite this morning’s better-than-expected sales data.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 is down 1%.

Thursday was a good day for UK government debt, which jumped in value after the Bank of England outlined an innovative plan for the government to buy some of its hard-to-sell bonds.

Today is not so good. Prices of gilts are falling, pushing up the yields of two, five, and 10-year bonds.

Under the BoE’s plan, the UK’s Debt Management Office would issue more shorter-dated bonds to fund the purchase of longer-dated debt from the BoE, which it has struggled to shift.

Investors may be calculating that the government will be issuing more short-term debt to fund this plan, and pricing that increase in supply into bond prices.

Lagarde pushes back on market rate-hike bets

The eurozone’s top central banker has tried to cool expectations that high energy costs will force the European Central Bank to keep raising interest rates.

Christine Lagarde told a news conference in Dublin:

double quotation mark “Interest rates do not move in lockstep with the price of energy because, obviously, the price of energy and its impact on prices has also an impact on other factors, including notably growth and consumption, and we factor in all these elements.”

Diesel prices across the UK’s forecourts are closing in on record levels.

RAC head of policy Simon Williams says:

double quotation mark “Unfortunately, it’s looking increasingly likely that the average price of diesel will reach a new all-time high next week as a litre now stands at 195.32p, just under 4p off the record of 199.09p set on 25 June 2022. “Diesel has risen nearly 12p (11.72p) this month, with 5p being added in the last week alone. The average price of petrol has now topped 172p (172.02p) having gone up more than 10p so far in September and 3.6p in the last week. The last time it was this high was 17 August 2022.

Investors expect the Bank of England to join the group of central bankers raising interest rates in November.

A hike at the BoE’s next meeting, on 5 November, is seen as a 65% chance this morning.

The most obvious factor determining whether this happens, or not, is whether there is progress to end the Iran war that pulls down the oil price.

After this morning’s losses the yen is trading at its lowest point against the US dollar in around two weeks.

The yen is defying the logic that a rise in interest rates should support a currency.

Instead, the yen has dropped to a two-week low against the dollar today. It’s down over 1% today to ¥157.90.

Traders are selling the yen after noting that two policy makers at the Bank of Japan declined to support today’s interest rate rise. That could limit the prospect of the BoJ raising interest rates faster.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, says BoJ governor Ueda has not sounded as hawkish as expected today:

double quotation mark Ueda has confused the market today with both hawkish and dovish signals, he has said that Japan is entering a new policy-making stage, but has also warned against rapid rate hikes that trigger asset price volatility. This highlights the BOJ’s dilemma, on the one hand they need to raise rates to stabilize inflation, but Japan has a huge government debt load and they cannot upset the bond market for fear of triggering global financial market instability. Anyone looking for Japanese funds and individuals to embark on mass capital repatriation on the back of this rate hike have been proved wrong, the yen is weaker today and Japanese bond yields are lower across the curve.

Some experts worry factors affecting wheat exports could push global food prices even higher than they are now

Wheat prices are at their highest level in three years, which means farmer Merrill Nielsen should be getting more for his crops out of his 2,500-acre (1,010-hectare) Kansas farm.

Yet even as future prices for bread-type wheat are up 39%, Nielsen is unsure whether increased prices will raise his bottom line. The price of diesel fuel, which he needs to run his tractor, has hit record highs. Then there’s the erratic weather that made him lose his entire wheat crop in the spring, and drought has overtaken the southern Great Plains.

“We’re not looking to plant any more wheat than we probably normally would, or maybe we won’t even plant that much. I don’t know. Really, we’ll have to see what the weather does for us,” Nielsen said.

The combination of high costs, poor weather and geopolitics leave US farmers such as Nielsen with an uncertain growing season despite higher prices for their yields. It also leaves consumers, from millers and bakers to restaurants and grocery shoppers, at risk of feeling the pinch.

Droughts across the US and Europe have been shriveling harvests, and weather forecasts for a “super” El Niño this year means “there are some alarming signals” about the impact of weather on wheat crops, said Joao Lampreia, a market strategist at the Lisbon-based Freedom24.

The weather phenomenon, exacerbated by the climate crisis, causes warm waters to rise to the surface across the equatorial Pacific Ocean, along the coast of South America, and is known to imperil agriculture in the southern hemisphere significantly. Experts say wheat supplies in key exporting countries are at their second-lowest levels on record. Already, Australia’s wheat plantings are down 12% due to expectations of dryness and increased fertilizer costs.

The good news for farmers and consumers is that El Niño can also bring wetter conditions for the southern Great Plains in the fall and spring. During the last big El Niño in 2015 and 2016, the US set an all-time record-high winter wheat yield, said Mark Welch, an economist who researches grain marketing at Texas A&M University.

Even if the weather impacts turn out better than expected, recent Russian attacks on port facilities in the Black Sea, where one-third of the global wheat trade passes through, have also disrupted grain shipments. Black Sea farmers, who were some of the few global wheat exporters to experience a bumper crop, had just wrapped up their harvest before the attacks.

Because of the fighting, supply is largely inaccessible, which has pushed prices up, Welch said. But if Black Sea farmers and shippers can find alternative routes, prices will backtrack somewhat.

At best, about 35% to 50% of that wheat could find a way out, but it will take longer and cost more to get, Lampreia said.

Dan Basse, president of the agricultural market research company AgResource, worries the that combination of weather-damaged harvests and the impact of geopolitics on wheat exports could leave global food prices even higher than they are today. The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization’s food price index , which tracks a basket of widely traded food commodities, was up 2.5% in August over a year ago, he said.

The spike in wheat prices “has tentacles that go far beyond the war between the Ukrainians and Russians”, Basse says. “The world needs more harvested acreage of every grain. All of this resonates in higher grain and food prices for the world looking forward.”

In the immediate future, US farmers will need to help make up the shortfall. Basse said he expected planted acreage for wheat this winter to expand about 10% more than last year as producers seek to capture higher prices.

But harvested acreage for wheat in the US has been at its lowest levels since 1877, as US farmers have found it more profitable to plant corn and soybeans rather than wheat. One year of high prices isn’t likely to change a structural decline.

Farmers will need higher production and strong values to benefit. “If it’s not an average yield or better, the breakeven cost really gets high very quickly,” Welch said.

And it’s unclear how much weather will continue to affect harvests. Vance Ehmke, a wheat-seed seller in south-west Kansas , said he’s been busy fielding more calls for seeds this year. But the weather in the southern Great Plains is now too dry for seeds to germinate and grow.

“If you get your wheat up, you’ve got 90% to 95% odds that you’ll harvest something. But if you can’t even get it up, I mean, you’re just screwed,” he said.

Prices will need to stay high to accommodate a surge in input prices, which have been exacerbated by ongoing trade wars. “We are the ones that get hurt by those policies,” Ehmke said.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to reform adult social care in England

Published 17 September 2026

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing calls to set a national waiting-time target for dementia care in England.

An Alzheimer's Society proposal to set an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target has been backed by Professor Sir Mike Richards, England's former national cancer director, and Baroness Louise Casey, who's leading a major review of adult social care.

In a report, Alzheimer's Society and the King's Trust said a "cancer-style revolution" was needed to improve dementia care, which they described as being "stuck in the 20th century".

In a speech at Alzheimer's Society conference on Thursday, Social Care Minister Alison McGovern expressed support for the report , external .

She said: "The report that the Alzheimer's Society published today on going on the journey that we've been on with cancer, with Alzheimer's and dementia, I think that's spot on."

The minister said dementia had been "neglected for far too long".

She added: "And nowhere is this division between health and social care felt more sharply than by people living with dementia in their families, too often left to navigate a shattered system at the most difficult time in their lives."

The government has committed to appointing a top official to oversee dementia care and publish a new plan - a modern service framework - to speed up support for those with the disease by the end of the year.

McGovern said the government would "appoint a dementia tsar, backed with real expertise".

Currently there is no waiting-time target for dementia in England.

In contrast, the NHS sets waiting-time targets for cancer diagnosis and treatment.

Professor Richards was the national cancer director when these cancer targets were introduced in 2000, and said he thought an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target for dementia patients was achievable.

He said setting such a target would require "political initiative" and extra funding.

"All of that is going to cost more money but remember the toll that this condition is taking at the moment, both on the people affected by dementia themselves and their relatives," the professor said.

The same proposal has been made by Baroness Casey.

In a letter to former Health Secretary Wes Streeting in March, she said the government should look at "how dementia can be put on a level playing field with other conditions, for example by setting national standards for dementia diagnosis, including an 18‑week referral‑to‑treatment target".

Speaking to the BBC, Baroness Casey said she agreed with the proposal to emulate cancer care.

She said: "I think the National Health Service and more generally all of us have stuck our heads in the sand about it, and it's time we started saying, yes, we should have a similar mission, and we should do as much as we possibly can on dementia, and now."

Baroness Casey is expected to publish her recommendations on social care reform next summer.

About one million people are living with dementia in the UK, a figure expected to reach 1.4 million by 2040.

Burnham cancelled his engagements earlier this week after the death of father, Roy, who had Alzheimer's disease.

Returning from compassionate leave, he said his father would have wanted him "back out there" to bring forward "the changes that he always pushed me to make".

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

Burnham has said he will wait for Baroness Casey's recommendations before deciding what changes to make to social care and how it's funded.

stories.title: UK needs 'credible path' on defence spending, says Nato chief
stories.summary: Mark Rutte tells the BBC that UK ministers accept the need to make yearly steps to up spending.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 September 2026

Nato chief Mark Rutte has said he is confident the UK government understands the need for a "credible path" to increase defence spending.

The alliance's secretary general told the BBC he was "absolutely confident" in the UK's commitment to hit a Nato-wide spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035.

Speaking after meetings in London, he said British ministers accepted the need to make yearly steps towards hitting the target.

But he accepted that the exact "pathway" towards the goal would not be set out until next year.

Andy Burnham has followed predecessor Sir Keir Starmer in committing to reach Nato's 3.5% spending target by 2035, up from an estimated 2.6% this year.

He has said date for reaching a planned 3% interim target will come next spring, when the long-term budgets of government departments are due to be set.

But he has faced pressure to immediately commit to reaching the milestone by the end of the decade. His chancellor and ex-defence secretary John Healey has previously argued this would show Britain was serious about the Nato goal.

Former Dutch PM Rutte has been encouraging members of the alliance not to pencil in large spending increases shortly before the deadline.

Speaking to BBC political editor Chris Mason after meeting Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in London, Rutte said he was confident British ministers understood the 2035 target could not be met "in one go in 2034".

"I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the 3.5[%] they are there," he said.

"I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there.

"There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year," he added.

'Tough decisions'

Rutte also said that defence spending should be separated out from the issue of welfare, adding that economic growth was the key to ensuring military commitments could be met alongside spending in other areas.

The Conservatives have been pushing for hikes in defence spending to be funded through cuts to benefits, and have criticised Burnham for saying last week that national security "can't come at the expense of social security".

Rutte added: "I don't know all the details of the UK economy, I think this is something this government is now navigating," he added.

"But I would say these are two separate issues."

"One is, indeed, spending on defence, but the other is of course making sure that the economy is growing enough, so you can distribute the success of a growing economy amongst various income groups, various issues in the Budget, for example welfare and healthcare and the pensions."

"You have to do it all, and if you want to do it successfully, you need economic growth," he added.

"Of course there are issues. I've been prime minister myself for 14 years. You have to take tough decisions, and it's not always easy."

Putin 'desperate'

“Let’s not be naive about what Putin could do”, Nato chief tells BBC

Elsewhere in his interview, Rutte said recent Russian military activity in western Ukraine which saw Poland close two of its airports on Thursday showed Vladimir Putin was "increasingly desperate" over his prospects for the war.

Asked about the possibility of a Russian attack that could demand a Nato response, he replied: "If you are willing to sacrifice 1.2 million of your own people in this crazy unprovoked fight, let's not be naïve about what Putin could do."

He also said there would be discussions among Nato allies over how to respond to the situation in the Red Sea, where Iran-aligned Houthis recently seized control of parts of Yemen's coast along the important shipping route.

Saudi Arabia has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

"I would not be surprised if some phone calls were taking place between European allies, 'hey, how are we going to deal with this?'" he added.

"Let's see what happens, and if Nato can help, we will always be helpful".

stories.body:
Published 16 September 2026

Unions who donate to Labour met John Healey on Thursday to press home their demands ahead of next month's Budget.

Unite, the UK's second biggest union, has called for a reversal of the freezing of tax thresholds, that see the lowest paid drawn into paying tax.

The call is one of a number of policy proposals unions have taken to the chancellor, including increased taxes on tech companies.

Unions say they believe Healey's first budget will define Andy Burnham's direction of travel as prime minister.

Burnham said the freezing of tax thresholds had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to return to Westminster as MP for Makerfield.

In her last Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves froze tax thresholds until 2031. The basic rate of 20% is paid on annual earnings between £12,571 and £50,270. The higher rate of 40% is paid on earnings between £50,271 and £125,140.

By not uprating those rates in line with inflation, more lower paid people have paid tax for the first time and more better-off workers, including public service workers such as senior nurses, police officers and teachers, are now paying tax at the higher rate.

Unite leader Sharon Graham said: "We must see things happen immediately. I told him [Burnham] that you have to make working class people believe their best days are in front of them.

"That tax threshold of around £12,500 - if that hadn't been frozen for the past few years it would have moved up to over £16,000 now. People at the lower end are paying eye-watering amounts of tax."

Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises Published 7 September

Burnham rejects 'tax and spend socialist' comments Published 1 day ago

Why the Budget means many will pay more tax Published 26 November 2025

The country's biggest union Unison is calling for the chancellor to increase tax on large tech companies to finance public sector investment and the transition to green energy.

It is also calling for the Treasury to commission research into whether the balance of taxation needs to move from income to wealth.

The union's general secretary Andrea Egan is not expecting dramatic change from Healey straight away at the Budget, but is expecting a new direction to be mapped out.

Her union is demanding that Labour makes clear it too is under new leadership and isn't just "continuity Starmer" with a more affable face.

The third biggest union, GMB, also has significant financial links to the Labour Party.

Leader Gary Smith has long advocated raising revenue from the oil and gas industries by approving the new Rosebank and Jackdaw fields in the North Sea.

A decision on whether these will go ahead seems unlikely until after the October by election in Sir Keir's former seat in north London - though the government maintains the timing is out of its hands as it is a quasi judicial decision.

Smith said: "The government really needs to get on with this.

"We are going to need oil and gas for generations to come. Rosebank and Jackdaw are good for jobs, good for the economy, but also good for the environment as we won't have to import so much from abroad as that is carbon intensive."

Smith also wants to see confidence building measures for the construction industry in the Budget.

He said: "We have half a million bricks stockpiled in this country - enough to build two Kidderminsters - and factories are being mothballed because we are not getting on with the house building programme. They have to cut through the red tape."

Following today's meeting, the BBC understands the chancellor will be speaking to industry experts, from business to trade unions, who will be key to reindustrialising the UK.

Healey made clear that tough choices where necessary will be taken but doubled down on his commitment to give businesses and workers a bit of breathing room where he can.

In the next couple of weeks, TUC officials and representatives of those unions which don't donate to Labour will also meet the chancellor.

TUC leader Paul Nowak told me his main demand was for Healey to reverse the last government's cut in the surcharge paid by banks to raise around £9bn to subsidise energy bills .

But he also wants to see the remit of the independent Budget watchdog, the OBR, revised, so it takes into account the value of long term investment and not just short term book-balancing.

Helen Jenner is Reform's deputy Welsh leader

Published 17 September 2026

Reform is likely to appoint Helen Jenner to take over from Dan Thomas as the party's Welsh leader, sources have told BBC Wales.

It is understood she is the favourite to replace Thomas, who quit following an arrest on suspicion of assault, and that "very senior" Reform figures had backed her.

Jenner, a Member of the Senedd for Bangor Conwy Môn, is the party's interim Welsh leader and was Thomas' deputy.

Thomas stood down after he was arrested and bailed by police at the weekend on suspicion of assault and controlling coercive behaviour.

He says he has done nothing wrong.

Meanwhile, chief whip Llŷr Powell told BBC Wales that he has ruled himself out of standing for the leadership.

Thomas has not been suspended and continues to represent Reform in the Senedd as MS for Casnewydd Islwyn.

Jenner is yet to speak publicly about her intentions.

The party's health spokesperson James Evans claimed on Wednesday he had majority support in the group but decided not to stand after speaking to his family.

If there is more than one candidate it is expected there will be a secret ballot of Reform MSs - but no vote of the membership.

Thomas was appointed by Nigel Farage in February.

Helen Jenner is a former English teacher who was born in the south Wales town of Neath and grew up on the island of Anglesey.

If she was confirmed as leader it would mean that, for the first time since devolution began in 1999, all party groups in the Senedd will be led by politicians from north Wales.

In a BBC Walescast podcast episode released during the summer Jenner, a Welsh speaker, said that people online had told her she had "no right" to attend the National Eisteddfod , because of her membership of Reform.

Jenner stood for the Brexit Party at the 2019 UK general election, and was previously a member of UKIP, when it was led by current Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

On Walescast she said Farage had helped her become engaged in politics.

"It was seeing him, and then watching his YouTube clips in the European Parliament and everything: I've never seen anybody so animated.

"I felt he was really principled and I suddenly thought 'oh, I actually care about politics now'."

No announcement is expected on the leadership on Friday.

stories.title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high
stories.summary: Rates are held for the sixth time in a row but the Bank of England says high energy prices make a future rise more likely.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 17 September 2026

The Bank of England has held interest rates at their current rate of 3.75% for the sixth time in a row but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.

The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted global energy supplies leading to a sharp increase in petrol and diesel prices and an uptick in inflation.

But Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.

The Bank also announced it was slowing its sales of UK government debt, prompting an easing in the UK's long-term borrowing costs.

The Bank of England's main interest rate is a crucial benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest rates for individuals and businesses who want to borrow or save money. Higher rates can help dampen inflationary pressures, while lower rates can help boost spending and investment.

The UK's central bank aims to keep inflation at a target of 2%, but it has been above that rate for nearly two years, with inflation hitting 3.1% in August .

On Thursday the Bank of England raised its forecast for inflation predicting it would be "slightly above 4%" at the start of next year. It warned that the price cap on household gas and electricity bills for January was "now expected to rise substantially further".

Speaking after the Bank's decision, Bailey said the direct impact of higher energy prices was clear, but officials were still assessing how far those costs would feed through into wider inflation across the economy.

Other major central banks have increased rates to counteract higher prices.

On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve announced its first hike in three years while the European Central Bank has raised rates twice since June.

Of the nine members on the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), six voted to hold rates at 3.75% while three - including the Bank's chief economist Huw Pill - wanted to raise them to 4%.

While financial markets have priced in the possibility of several rate rises next year, Bailey said the global backdrop remained "hugely unpredictable at the moment".

He said that for interest rates to come down there would need to be "an end of conflict in the Middle East... and energy prices coming really back to where they were before this conflict began".

There were some positive notes from the Bank of England.

It said the UK economy had been "more resilient" than it had expected and raised its prediction for economic growth from 0.1% to 0.4% for the period between July and September.

It also said that because the effect of higher energy costs had not yet spilled over into other areas of the economy, food price inflation was now predicted to be 4% by the end of the year, less than the Bank's previous forecast of 6-7%.

Given the global picture, and market expectations of a higher Bank rate, a host of major lenders have already increased the cost of new fixed-rate mortgages.

The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate is at its highest since 11 May, at 5.77%, while the average five-year is at its highest since 8 November 2023, at 5.83%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.

'Knock-on effect'

The move will have a significant effect on borrowers like Andy Pargeter from Flintshire and his wife. They are coming off a five-year fixed rate mortgage of 1.19% in November. Earlier in the year they had hoped that interest rates might be falling at this point. However with rates held steady they now expect to pay around £300 more a month.

"We're in a fortunate position where we're able to accommodate that [increase]," he told BBC News. But he expects it will have "a knock-on effect in terms of how much we potentially save every month".

"It's definitely been something… I have constantly been thinking about."

Bond sales paused

Alongside the interest rate decision, the Bank also said it would halt its so-called "quantitative tightening" (QT) programme.

It will pause its annual sale of government bonds – which are a kind of IOU that can be traded on the financial markets – and will instead sell off smaller chunks over eight years.

The Bank bought £895bn of mainly government bonds during periods of economic turbulence such as the global financial crisis and the Covid pandemic to help keep the economy on an even keel. This was known as "quantitative easing".

Since 2022, it has been offloading the bonds, including through sales. This has contributed to higher interest rates – or yields – on bonds, making it more expensive for the government to borrow money.

The Bank said discussions to put in place a plan to reduce the current £488bn stockpile of bonds had started a year ago, implying the decision was not related to the recent rise in long term borrowing costs.

The news that the Bank of England is overhauling its QT programme prompted an immediate reaction.

The yield on 30-year UK government bonds fell from 5.86% on Thursday morning to 5.75% following the Bank's announcement. Yields on 10-year bonds dropped from 5.31% to 5.22%.

stories.title: Conservatives urge Burnham to rule out tax rises at Budget
stories.summary: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith says rumours of further taxes are "causing Britain's wealth creators to flee the country".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andrew Griffith was appointed shadow chancellor by Tory leader Kemi Badenoch

Published 17 September 2026

The Conservatives are urging Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey to rule out tax rises at next month's Budget.

In his first major speech as shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said businesses were "suffering enough" and that rumours of higher taxes were "causing Britain's wealth creators to flee the country".

He also promised to replace tax rules for self-employed workers, who he said had been "badly let down" by the system.

Labour said: "Andrew Griffith has made the Conservatives' priorities clear: scrapping hard-won workers' rights, while promising tax cuts with no explanation of how they would pay for them or which public services would be cut."

The Labour spokesperson added: "The Tories should be apologising for crashing the economy thanks to Griffith's old boss Liz Truss – not asking working people to pay the price all over again."

The chancellor is due to set out his Budget on 28 October against a backdrop of rising inflation and global energy prices.

On Thursday, trade unions will meet the chancellor to push for their proposals, with the Unite union urging the government to reverse the freezing of tax thresholds.

Burnham has warned that the Budget would be "challenging" due to the war in the Middle East but insisted he was prepared to take "difficult decisions" on the economy.

Call to raise tax thresholds among union demands ahead of Budget Published 20 hours ago

Burnham rejects 'tax and spend socialist' comments Published 1 day ago

Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises Published 7 September

Griffith - who was appointed as shadow chancellor last month - told an audience at a further education college that taxes in the UK had reached "nosebleed territory" and that Healey "must end uncertainty today and rule out any new taxes".

"He must rule out increasing taxes on small businesses and the self-employed."

Griffith described business owners and the self-employed as "economic heroes", adding: "Any government worth its salt would do everything it could to help them because whilst not every acorn grows into a mighty oak we need green shoots that are nurtured not trampled upon."

He said the IR35 regime had "crushed the dreams of self-employed people" and promised that a Conservative government would "replace it with a new system that respects the right of the self-employed to choose their status and only prevents actual abuse".

The IR35 rules are designed to prevent people avoiding tax by posing as self-employed contractors rather than employees but some freelancers argue the system has led to unfair treatment.

Griffith also urged the chancellor to pause the rollout of Making Tax Digital, the new system for the self-employed to register their income with HMRC.

"For the self-employed, many of whom will have started out in colleges such as this, there is this special torture of Making Tax Digital."

He acknowledged that the previous Conservative government had been responsible for setting up the system and said that "despite well-intentioned, the execution has left a lot to be desired".

Griffith told the audience that he had commissioned Lord Mackinlay of Richborough, the former South Thanet MP , and Robert Colvile, the outgoing director of the Centre for Policy Studies think tank, to produce a report on reducing regulations for small businesses.

Over the weekend, the Mail on Sunday reported , external that the Conservatives could promise to abolish inheritance tax if they win the next election, with the policy potentially being announced at the party's annual conference in October.

Speaking to the BBC ahead of his speech, Griffith said he would "love" to cut the tax but it would have to be "subject to an ability to set out properly how we would fund that".

"I'm going to be responsible and only want to make promises I can keep," he said.

He added that he had recently been on a fact-finding trip to Sweden, which scrapped inheritance taxes in 2005.

Reform UK has previously said it wanted to cut inheritance tax, but speaking at the party's conference, the party's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said it would not be a priority.

"It's a bold chancellor that would say I'd rather privilege 36,000 families than 40 million [income] taxpayers," he told a Reform conference fringe event.

Asked if getting rid of inheritance tax would amount to a tax cut for the wealthy, Griffith argued that it would boost growth and that the wealthiest people were often able to "arrange their affairs" to avoid the tax.

stories.title: Rayner to rule on landmark green belt appeal
stories.summary: Campaigners say their Albrighton appeal could shape future green belt decisions.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The appeal centres on land off Patshull Road near Albrighton

Published 17 September 2026

The fate of a controversial plan for 800 homes on green belt land near a Shropshire village will be decided by Housing Secretary Angela Rayner in a case campaigners say could test Labour's planning reforms.

A 12-day appeal is underway into whether Boningale Homes should be allowed to build the estate south of Albrighton after Shropshire Council rejected the application.

Instead of being determined by the planning inspector overseeing the appeal, the government told the council on Wednesday that Rayner would make the final decision.

A letter sent on her behalf said the appeal raised "important or novel issues" and involved "significant development in the green belt".

The case centres on land off Patshull Road, which Boningale Homes argues should be considered "grey belt" rather than green belt.

Under planning reforms introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's Labour government, some lower-quality or underused green belt sites could be released for development to help boost housebuilding.

The government is aiming to build 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, although ministers have acknowledged the target will be difficult to achieve.

Speaking on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Rayner said there was only a "slim chance" of meeting it by 2029.

Campaigners say the appeal could become a key test of green belt planning policy

Campaigners opposed to the development said they had long argued the appeal was of national importance because of what it could mean for future green belt decisions elsewhere in England.

The Albrighton Development Action Group (ADAG) described it as "the biggest test case of its type to date".

"If we are successful, then we will give confidence to hundreds of places across the country that their vital open spaces and productive farmland can be protected for their children now and for the generations to come," a spokesperson said.

The group said it remained confident that both the planning inspector and Rayner would dismiss the appeal.

It argued the site remained "productive farmland and core green belt" and should continue to be protected from development.

Conservative MP Mark Pritchard has criticised the government's decision to determine the appeal

The area's Conservative MP, Mark Pritchard, criticised the government's intervention, describing it as "chillingly egregious".

"It is in many ways ideologically driven, which is possibly one of the most worrying things of all," he said.

"Who knows, she might pleasantly surprise me, but I'm afraid her track record [for building homes] is not boding well for Shropshire."

Boningale Homes declined to comment while the appeal hearing is ongoing.

Sadiq Khan stumps Polanski by addressing him in Urdu in London assembly, mocking Green leader's byelection video

Zack Polanski , the Green leader who is standing as his party’s candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, has recorded a short campaign video in Urdu . Katie Lam , the shadow communities secretary, has described this as “poisonous” and said the Tories would ban candidates from campaigning in foreign languages. Even Jonathan Reynolds , the business secretary, has said the video made him feel “uncomfortable”.

Polanski is a member of the London assembly and today Sadiq Khan , the Labour mayor, was appearing before the assembly to take questions. As Polanski asked him a question about data centres, Khan, whose parents came to the UK from Pakistan, mocked him by replying in Urdu.
